newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM backs move to end euthanasia law.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM backs move to end euthanasia law.

text.p: The world's first voluntary euthanasia law faced a fresh challenge on Monday as Australia's parliament considered a plan, endorsed by Prime Minister John Howard, to overturn it.

Howard said he would vote for a bill tabled by government backbencher Kevin Andrews in parliament's lower house on Monday aimed at over-riding the assisted suicide law that took effect in the Northern Territory in July.
"It is a matter of principle," Howard said in a radio interview. "It goes to the essence of what we see life to be and the sanctity of it and the importance of it and the quality of it."
Despite his opposition to the assisted suicide law, Howard will allow a conscience vote on the bill and not demand his colleagues toe a party line.

"I've stated my position on euthanasia in the past. I don't intend to force that view down the throats of any of my colleagues," he said. "This is a very difficult, sensitive issue and there are passionately held views on both sides."
Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley has also condemned the law, but is allowing his colleagues a conscience vote.
The territory law allows doctors to help terminally-ill patients kill themselves with a lethal injection or pills.
Tabling his bill, which has to be approved by both houses of parliament, Andrews said the territory government had legalised intentional killing in a move that affected all Australians.
"Every other state and territory has laws which proscribe intentional killing and assisted suicide," Andrews told parliament's lower house, the House of Representatives.
The bill is expected to be voted on during the current parliamentary session, which ends in December, but Andrews said the timing depended on the upper house, the Senate.
The euthanasia law took effect in July but has not yet been used, with doctors unsure of their legal position in the face of court and parliamentary challenges to the law.

Separate efforts to strike out the law through the territory's parliament and supreme court failed earlier this year, but the law still faces a constitutional challenge in the country's top court, the High Court.
The voluntary euthanasia law has sparked strong condemnation from political, church, aboriginal and community leaders, but opinion polls show strong public support.
Euthanasia is illegal in Australia's other territory and six states, but doctors say it is unofficially practised.
Andrews told reporters the territory law, which is not restricted to territory residents, was open to abuse.
"Once you allow intentional killing and assisted suicide, you cross a line and thereafter it's virtually impossible to draw another line," Andrews said outside parliament.
Australia's national government has the power to over-ride laws in the country's two territories, but not the six states.
Howard rejected criticism over the national government over-riding territory legislation.

"The law allows a territory law to be over-ridden by the federal parliament, so we're not acting unconstitutionally or improperly or indecently, we're exercising the lawful power currently given to the national parliament," he said.
